tool.name: HTML
tool.tagline: The markup language that gives every web page its structure and meaning
tool.description: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the content of a web page: headings, text, links, images, forms and the regions of a layout. Browsers parse it into the DOM that CSS styles and JavaScript scripts. Writing clean, semantic HTML is the foundation of accessible, fast and search-friendly websites.

concepts.name: Document structure
concepts.summary: Every page starts from the same skeleton: a doctype, an html element with a language, a head for metadata and a body for content.
concepts.why: Getting the skeleton right switches browsers into standards mode and sets encoding and language for everything that follows.
concepts.body:
An HTML file is plain text that a browser parses into a tree. Every page should start with the same few lines.

- `<!DOCTYPE html>` comes first. It's not a tag but a switch: without it browsers fall back to **quirks mode**, emulating 1990s layout bugs.
- `<html lang="en">` is the root element. The `lang` attribute tells screen readers how to pronounce text, and helps translation tools and search engines.
- `<head>` holds information *about* the page: the character encoding, the `<title>` shown in the browser tab, links to stylesheets, and meta tags.
- `<body>` holds everything the user sees.

Put `<meta charset="utf-8">` as the first thing in the head. The browser must know the encoding before it reads any text, and UTF-8 covers every language and emoji.

The `<title>` is required for a valid document and matters more than it looks: it's the tab label, the default bookmark name, and usually the headline in search results.

Indentation and line breaks between tags don't affect the layout; HTML collapses runs of whitespace in text to a single space. Save the file as `index.html`, open it in a browser, and use the developer tools (right-click, Inspect) to see the tree the browser built.
concepts.code:
Hello, web

This paragraph is the visible content.
takeaways: Start every page with <!DOCTYPE html> to get standards mode
head = metadata about the page, body = visible content
Declare <meta charset="utf-8"> first and set lang on <html>
pitfalls: Leaving out the doctype and debugging layout bugs caused by quirks mode.

quiz.q: What happens if a page omits <!DOCTYPE html>?
options: The browser renders it in quirks mode
quiz.explain: Without the doctype browsers use quirks mode, which emulates legacy layout behaviour.

quiz.q: Where does the text in <title> appear?
options: In the browser tab and in search results
As the first heading of the page body
Nowhere; it is only for validators
quiz.explain: The title labels the tab and bookmarks and is typically the search result headline.

concepts.name: Elements and attributes
concepts.summary: Elements are built from tags that wrap content and nest inside each other; attributes add extra information to an element.
concepts.why: Every other HTML lesson is just a new element or attribute applied with these rules.

An **element** usually has an opening tag, content and a closing tag: `

Quote values (double quotes are the convention). **Boolean attributes** are true by being present: `` is disabled, and `disabled="false"` is still disabled. A few **global attributes** work on any element: - `id` gives a unique name, used by links, labels, CSS and JavaScript. - `class` holds space-separated names for styling groups of elements. - `hidden` hides the element; `title` adds a tooltip; `lang` overrides the language. - `data-*` attributes such as `data-user-id="42"` store your own data for scripts. concepts.name: Links
concepts.summary: The a element with href links to other pages, sections of the same page, email addresses and downloads.
concepts.why: Links are what make the web a web; getting URLs and link text right affects usability, SEO and security.
concepts.body:
A link is an `<a>` element with an `href`. The `href` can be:

- an **absolute URL** like `https://example.com/docs`,
- a **root-relative** path like `/about` (from the site's root),
- a **relative** path like `pricing.html` or `../index.html` (from the current page's folder),
- a **fragment** like `#faq`, which scrolls to the element with `id="faq"`,
- a scheme such as `mailto:hi@example.com` or `tel:+15551234`.

Write **link text** that makes sense on its own: "Read the pricing guide", not "click here". Screen-reader users often list all links on a page, and search engines use the text to understand the target.

`target="_blank"` opens a new tab. Modern browsers imply `rel="noopener"` for it, so the new page can't control yours via `window.opener`, but use it sparingly; people can open new tabs themselves. Use `rel="nofollow"` or `rel="sponsored"` for untrusted or paid links.

The `download` attribute asks the browser to save the target instead of navigating to it (same-origin only).

A link navigates; a button does something on the current page. If clicking runs JavaScript and doesn't go anywhere, use `<button>`, not `<a href="#">`. Wrapping a whole card in an `<a>` is allowed, since `<a>` may contain block content, as long as there are no other interactive elements inside.

takeaways: href takes absolute, root-relative, relative or #fragment URLs
Link text should describe the destination
Use <a> to navigate and <button> to perform actions
pitfalls: Using <a href="#" onclick=...> for actions; it breaks keyboard and screen-reader expectations.

quiz.q: A page at https://site.com/blog/post.html has <a href="../about">. Where does it go?
quiz.explain: The relative path starts in /blog/, and ../ goes up one folder to the root.

concepts.name: Images
concepts.summary: Embed pictures with img, always describing them with alt text and giving width and height to avoid layout shifts.
concepts.why: Images are most of a page's bytes, and missing alt text is the most common accessibility failure on the web.
concepts.body: `` embeds an image. It's a void element, and two of its attributes deserve real thought. **alt** is the text alternative, read by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. Describe what the image *conveys* in context: "Bar chart: sales doubled in 2025", not "chart.png". If an image is purely decorative, use an empty `alt=""` so assistive technology skips it. Leaving out `alt` entirely is worse: screen readers may read the file name. **width and height** in pixels (unitless numbers) let the browser reserve the right space before the image downloads. Without them, text jumps down when images load, which is the layout shift Core Web Vitals penalise. CSS can still resize the image; the browser uses the attributes for the aspect ratio. Pick formats sensibly: - JPEG or WebP/AVIF for photos, - PNG or WebP for screenshots with sharp edges and transparency, - SVG for logos, icons and diagrams, since it scales without blur. For a caption, wrap the image in `
takeaways: Every img needs alt: a description, or alt="" if decorative
Set width and height to prevent layout shift
Use figure and figcaption for captions
loading="lazy" for below-the-fold images only
pitfalls: Lazy-loading the hero image at the top of the page, which delays the most important paint.

quiz.q: An icon next to the text 'Settings' inside a button is purely visual. What alt should it have?
quiz.explain: The adjacent text already labels the button, so the icon is decorative and gets an empty alt.

concepts.name: Block, inline and generic containers
concepts.summary: Understand block versus inline flow and when the generic div and span containers are the right choice.
concepts.why: Knowing how elements flow by default explains most surprises before you write any CSS.
concepts.body:
By default, elements fall into two flow behaviours (CSS controls this through `display`, but the browser's defaults come from the element). - **Block-level** elements such as `

`, `

`, `
    `, `
    ` and `
    ` start on a new line and stretch to the full available width. - **Inline** elements such as ``, ``, ``, ``, `` and `` sit inside a line of text and are only as wide as their content. HTML also restricts what can go where. A `

    ` can only contain inline (phrasing) content: if you put a `

    ` or `
      ` inside a paragraph, the parser closes the paragraph early and you get an empty `

      ` you didn't write. A `

        ` may only have `
      • ` children. When no element describes your content, use the **generic containers**: `
        ` (block) and `` (inline). They mean nothing; they exist as hooks for CSS classes and scripts. That's their strength and their danger. A page built only from `
        ` works visually but tells browsers, search engines and screen readers nothing about its structure. So reach for a meaningful element first (heading, list, nav, button, article), and use `
        ` and `` for purely presentational grouping, such as a wrapper you need for a flex layout or a span to colour one word.

concepts.name: Forms, inputs and labels
concepts.summary: Collect user input with form, input, label and button, and send it to a server with name/value pairs.
concepts.why: Forms are how users sign up, search, pay and talk to almost every web application.
concepts.body:
A `<form>` groups controls and sends their values when submitted. Its `action` is the URL to send to and `method` is `get` (values in the query string; for searches and filters) or `post` (values in the request body; for anything that changes data).

Each control needs a `name`: only named controls are submitted, as `name=value` pairs. The common controls:

- `<input type="text">` and its many types (email, password, number, checkbox, radio...),
- `<textarea>` for multi-line text,
- `<select>` with `<option>` elements for a choice list,
- `<button>` to submit.

Every control needs a **label**. Either wrap the control in `<label>` or connect them with `for` matching the control's `id`. A label is announced by screen readers, and clicking it focuses the control or toggles the checkbox, which makes small targets easier to hit. A `placeholder` is not a label: it disappears as soon as the user types.

Radio buttons that share a `name` form one group where only one can be selected; group related controls in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` describing the question.

A `<button>` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`. For a button that should only run JavaScript, write `type="button"`, or it will submit the form. Pressing Enter in a text field also submits the form.
concepts.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <label>
    Password <input name="password" type="password" minlength="8" required>
  </label>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Plan</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" checked> Free</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro"> Pro</label>
  </fieldset>

  <label><input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes"> Send me news</label>

  <button>Create account</button>   <!-- type="submit" by default -->
</form>
<!-- Sends: email=...&password=...&plan=free (&news=yes only if checked) -->
takeaways: Only controls with a name are submitted
Every control needs a label (wrapping or for/id)
method=get for reads, post for changes
A button in a form submits unless type="button"
pitfalls: Using placeholder text instead of a label.
A plain <button> meant for JavaScript accidentally submitting the form.

quiz.q: A form has <input id="q"> with no name attribute. What is sent for it on submit?
options: An error is shown to the user
quiz.explain: Only controls with a name are included in the submitted data.

concepts.name: Semantic page layout
concepts.summary: Use header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer to describe the regions of a page instead of anonymous divs.
concepts.why: Landmark elements give screen-reader users a map of the page and make your markup self-documenting.
concepts.body:
HTML has elements for the typical regions of a page. They look exactly like `<div>` until styled, but they carry meaning.

- `<header>`: introductory content, usually a logo, site title and navigation. Can also head an article.
- `<nav>`: a block of major navigation links. Not every group of links; the main menu, a table of contents, pagination.
- `<main>`: the page's primary content. Exactly one visible `<main>` per page, not inside header, footer or article.
- `<article>`: a self-contained piece that would make sense on its own: a blog post, a comment, a product card.
- `<section>`: a thematic group of content, normally with its own heading. If you can't think of a heading, you probably want a `<div>`.
- `<aside>`: tangentially related content, like a sidebar or callout.
- `<footer>`: closing information, such as copyright, contact links or an article's author info.

Browsers expose many of these as **landmarks**: a screen-reader user can jump straight to `main` or to the navigation, skipping repetitive content. `header` and `footer` count as page landmarks only when they aren't nested inside an article or section.

Other useful semantic elements are `<time datetime="2026-10-17">` for machine-readable dates, `<address>` for contact info of the page or article author, and `<search>` for a search region. Semantics also feed reader modes, browser features and search engines, so they pay off in many places at once.

Acme
Products Blog

Shipping our new API

Published 17 October 2026

What changed

...

Related posts...
© 2026 Acme
takeaways: Landmarks (header, nav, main, aside, footer) let users jump around a page
One main per page
article = stands alone; section = themed part with a heading
pitfalls: Wrapping every chunk in <section> without a heading; use div for pure styling groups.

quiz.q: Which element fits a single user comment under a blog post best?
quiz.explain: A comment is self-contained content that could be syndicated on its own, which is what article means.

concepts.name: Tables
concepts.summary: Present tabular data with table, caption, thead, tbody, th and td, using scope so headers are announced correctly.
concepts.why: Tables are the right tool for data with rows and columns, and the wrong tool for layout.
concepts.body:
Use a `<table>` when data really has two dimensions: a price list, a schedule, comparison data. Never use tables for page layout; that's what CSS grid and flexbox are for.

The structure:

- `<caption>` as the first child gives the table a title, announced by screen readers.
- `<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>` group header, body and summary rows.
- `<tr>` is a row; `<th>` is a header cell and `<td>` a data cell.

Mark headers with `<th>` and add `scope="col"` or `scope="row"` so assistive technology knows which data cells each header labels. When a reader lands on a cell, it can then say "Price, Pro plan: $12" instead of just "$12".

Cells can span: `colspan="2"` stretches a cell across two columns and `rowspan="3"` down three rows. Complex spanning makes tables hard to read and navigate; often two simple tables are clearer.

Even if you leave out `<tbody>`, the parser inserts one, which matters when you write CSS like `table > tr` (it won't match). Wide tables overflow small screens: wrap the table in a `<div>` styled with `overflow-x: auto` so it scrolls horizontally instead of breaking the layout.
concepts.code:
Plans and prices (per month)
Plan Price Projects
Free$03
Pro$12Unlimited
Prices exclude VAT.
takeaways: Tables are for tabular data only, never layout
Use caption, thead/tbody and th with scope
colspan/rowspan merge cells; keep spanning simple
pitfalls: Styling `table > tr` and wondering why nothing matches: the parser inserted a tbody.

quiz.q: What does scope="row" on a th do?
options: Marks the cell as the header for the data cells in its row
Makes the cell span the entire row
quiz.explain: scope tells assistive technology which cells a header labels.

concepts.name: Input types and built-in validation
concepts.summary: Pick specialised input types and use required, pattern, min, max and length limits to validate without JavaScript.
concepts.why: The right input type gives mobile users the right keyboard and gets you free validation and pickers.
concepts.body:
`<input>` has over twenty `type` values, and choosing well improves forms immediately.

- `email`, `url`, `tel`: on phones these bring up keyboards with `@`, `/` or digits. email and url are also validated.
- `number` (with `min`, `max`, `step`), `range` for a slider, `date`, `time`, `datetime-local`, `month`: native pickers.
- `checkbox`, `radio`, `color`, `file` (with `accept="image/*"` and `multiple`), `search`, `password`, `hidden`.

**Constraint attributes** let the browser validate before submitting: `required`, `minlength`/`maxlength`, `min`/`max`, `step`, and `pattern` (a regular expression that must match the whole value). On submit, the first invalid field gets focus and a native message. The CSS pseudo-classes `:invalid` and `:user-invalid` style fields; `:user-invalid` only applies after the user has interacted, so empty required fields aren't red on page load.

`autocomplete` tokens such as `email`, `name`, `street-address`, `new-password`, `current-password` and `one-time-code` let browsers and password managers fill fields correctly. `inputmode="numeric"` asks for a digit keyboard without number semantics, which is better than `type="number"` for things like card numbers and postcodes, where arrows and scroll-wheel changes make no sense.

Client-side validation is a convenience for users, not security. Anyone can bypass it, so the server must validate everything again.
concepts.code:
<form>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required></label>

  <label>Age <input type="number" name="age" min="13" max="120" step="1"></label>

  <label>Postcode
    <input name="zip" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{5}" autocomplete="postal-code"
           title="Five digits">
  </label>

  <label>Start date <input type="date" name="start" min="2026-01-01"></label>

  <label>Avatar <input type="file" name="avatar" accept="image/*"></label>

  <label>New password
    <input type="password" name="pw" minlength="12" autocomplete="new-password" required>
  </label>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
takeaways: Specific input types give the right mobile keyboard and native pickers
required, pattern, min/max and minlength validate before submit
autocomplete tokens help browsers fill forms
Always validate again on the server
pitfalls: Using type="number" for card numbers or postcodes; use inputmode="numeric" with pattern.

quiz.q: An input has pattern="[0-9]{3}". Which value passes validation?
quiz.explain: pattern must match the whole value, so exactly three digits.

concepts.name: Head metadata and SEO
concepts.summary: Fill the head with the viewport, description, icons, canonical URL and social-preview tags that browsers and crawlers rely on.
concepts.why: Missing head tags are why sites look tiny on phones, show ugly link previews or rank poorly.
concepts.body:
Beyond `charset` and `title`, a few head tags belong on every page.

- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tells mobile browsers to use the device width. Without it, phones render the page at about 980px wide and shrink it, so text is unreadable and media queries don't fire as expected.
- `<meta name="description" content="...">` is the snippet search engines often show under your title. Write one sentence per page.
- `<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">` sets the tab icon; add `<link rel="apple-touch-icon">` for home screens.
- `<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page">` names the preferred URL when the same content is reachable at several URLs.
- `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">` loads CSS. Stylesheets in the head block rendering, which is what you want for the main CSS.

**Open Graph** tags (`og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`, `og:url`) control the preview card when someone shares the link in chat apps and social networks; `twitter:card` refines it on X.

`<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` keeps a page out of search results. `<meta name="theme-color">` tints browser UI on mobile. Note that `<meta name="keywords">` has been ignored by major search engines for years, so don't bother.
concepts.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Pricing · Acme</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Simple pricing for teams of any size. Start free.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.example/pricing">
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/site.css">

  <!-- link previews in chat apps and social networks -->
  <meta property="og:title" content="Acme pricing">
  <meta property="og:description" content="Start free, upgrade when you grow.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.example/og/pricing.png">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://acme.example/pricing">
  <meta name="theme-color" content="#0f172a">
</head>
takeaways: The viewport meta is mandatory for mobile-friendly pages
Write a unique title and description per page
canonical picks one URL for duplicate content
Open Graph tags control link previews
pitfalls: Forgetting the viewport meta and then fighting media queries that never seem to apply on phones.

quiz.q: A page looks zoomed-out and tiny on phones although it has media queries. What's the most likely cause?
options: The CSS file is too large
The viewport meta tag is missing
quiz.explain: Without the viewport meta, mobile browsers lay out at a desktop width and scale down.

concepts.name: Accessibility fundamentals
concepts.summary: Make pages usable for everyone: native elements, keyboard access, visible focus, text alternatives and correct names for controls.
concepts.why: Accessible HTML is a legal requirement in many places and makes sites better for all users.
concepts.body:
Accessibility (a11y) means people using screen readers, keyboards, voice control or zoom can use your page. Most of it comes free when you use the right element.

**Use native elements.** A `<button>` is focusable, activates with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. A `<div onclick>` does none of that. The same goes for links, inputs, checkboxes and selects.

**Everything works by keyboard.** Tab moves through links, buttons and form controls in DOM order. Never remove the focus outline without replacing it (style `:focus-visible` instead), and keep the source order logical rather than rearranging visually with CSS.

**Every control has an accessible name**: from its text content, its `<label>`, or `alt` for images. An icon-only button needs a name, for example visually hidden text or `aria-label="Close"`.

**Structure is navigation**: a sensible heading hierarchy, landmarks (`main`, `nav`), and lists for lists. Screen-reader users jump by these.

Other essentials:

- Set `lang` on `<html>`.
- Don't convey meaning by colour alone; add text or icons.
- Keep text contrast at least 4.5:1 (WCAG AA).
- Add captions to video.
- Add a "skip to content" link as the first focusable element.

Test by unplugging the mouse and tabbing through the page, and by running the browser's Lighthouse or accessibility inspector. Automated tools catch roughly a third of issues; keyboard and screen-reader testing finds the rest.

concepts.name: Responsive images
concepts.summary: Serve the right image file for each screen with srcset and sizes, and switch formats or crops with picture.
concepts.why: Sending a 3000-pixel image to a phone wastes bandwidth and slows the page more than almost anything else.
concepts.body: One image file can't suit both a phone and a 4K monitor. HTML lets you offer several and let the browser choose. **Resolution switching** with `srcset` and `sizes`: list candidate files with their intrinsic widths (`photo-480.jpg 480w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w`), and tell the browser how wide the image will be displayed with `sizes`, a list of media conditions and lengths like `(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw`. The browser multiplies that width by the device pixel ratio and downloads the smallest adequate file. It needs `sizes` because it picks the image before CSS layout is known. Without `sizes` it assumes `100vw`. For fixed-size images, such as an 80px avatar, use density descriptors instead: `srcset="a.jpg 1x, a@2x.jpg 2x"`. **The picture element** handles two other cases: - **Format switching**: `` and `` before the fallback ``; the browser takes the first type it supports. - **Art direction**: `` serves a different crop on narrow screens. The `` inside `` is required: it's what actually renders, and it carries `alt`, `width`, `height` and `loading`. The `` elements only supply alternative URLs.
takeaways: srcset with w descriptors + sizes = browser picks the right resolution
Use 1x/2x descriptors for fixed-size images
picture + source switches formats or crops; the inner img still renders
pitfalls: Leaving out sizes with w descriptors, so the browser assumes 100vw and downloads files that are too big.

quiz.q: Why does the browser need the sizes attribute with srcset width descriptors?
options: It sets the CSS width of the image
It's required for alt text to work
It chooses an image before layout, so it needs to know the display width in advance
It tells the server how to resize the image
quiz.explain: Image selection happens early, before CSS layout is known, so sizes supplies the expected display width.

concepts.name: Video, audio and embeds
concepts.summary: Embed media with video and audio elements, add captions with track, and embed other pages safely with iframe.
concepts.why: Native media elements replace plugins and work everywhere, but captions and iframe sandboxing are easy to forget.
concepts.body:
`<video>` and `<audio>` play media natively.

- `controls` shows the browser's player UI. Without it, the user can't play or pause unless you build controls.
- Offer several encodings with `<source src type>` children; the browser plays the first it supports. MP4 (H.264) plays everywhere; WebM or AV1 are smaller.
- `poster` sets a preview image; `preload="none"` or `"metadata"` saves bandwidth.
- Browsers block autoplay with sound. `autoplay` only works reliably with `muted`, and `playsinline` keeps iOS from going full-screen.

**Captions** come from a `<track kind="captions" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">` pointing at a WebVTT file. They're essential for deaf users and for anyone watching without sound.

An `<iframe>` embeds another page, like a map, a video player or a payment widget. It's a whole browsing context, so treat it with care:

- Give it a `title` describing its content, for screen readers.
- `loading="lazy"` defers off-screen embeds, which are often heavy.
- `sandbox` restricts the embedded page; add back only what it needs, e.g. `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"`.
- `allow` grants features such as `fullscreen` or `autoplay`.

Sites can refuse to be framed with the `X-Frame-Options` or CSP `frame-ancestors` headers, which is why some URLs show an error inside an iframe.
takeaways: Add controls, multiple sources and a poster to video
Autoplay only works muted
Captions via track and WebVTT
Give iframes a title, lazy-load them, and sandbox untrusted ones
pitfalls: Expecting autoplay with sound to work; browsers block it until the user interacts.

quiz.q: A hero video with autoplay doesn't start in Chrome. What's the likely fix?
quiz.explain: Browsers allow autoplay only for muted media (or after user interaction).

concepts.name: Loading scripts: defer, async, module
concepts.summary: Control when JavaScript downloads and runs with defer, async and type=module, and hint important resources with preload.
concepts.why: A single misplaced script tag can block rendering for seconds; the right attribute fixes it for free.
concepts.body:
A plain `<script src="app.js">` in the head is **parser-blocking**: the browser stops building the page, downloads the script, runs it, then continues. Users stare at a blank screen meanwhile. Two attributes fix this for external scripts.

- `defer`: download in parallel with parsing, run after the document is parsed, in document order, before `DOMContentLoaded`. Right for almost all app code, because the DOM is ready when it runs.
- `async`: download in parallel and run as soon as it arrives, in any order, possibly before parsing finishes. Right for independent scripts like analytics.

`<script type="module">` loads an ES module. Modules are **deferred by default**, run in strict mode, can `import` other modules, and run once even if included twice. Add `async` to a module to run it as soon as it and its imports are ready. `<script nomodule>` is a fallback for browsers without module support, which today is effectively none.

Inline scripts without `src` ignore `defer` and run immediately (unless they're modules).

**Resource hints** in the head speed up loading:

- `<link rel="preload" href="font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>`: fetch something needed soon that the browser would discover late.
- `<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/chart.js">`: preload a module and its parsing.
- `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example">`: open the connection early.

Overusing preload backfires: everything preloaded competes for bandwidth with what's actually critical.
concepts.code:
<head>
  <!-- Blocks parsing until downloaded and run: avoid -->
  <!-- <script src="/js/app.js"></script> -->

  <!-- Runs after parsing, in order: good default for app code -->
  <script src="/js/vendor.js" defer></script>
  <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- Runs whenever it arrives: independent third-party code -->
  <script src="https://analytics.example/a.js" async></script>

  <!-- ES module: deferred automatically -->
  <script type="module" src="/js/main.js"></script>

  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
  <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
</head>
takeaways: Plain scripts in the head block parsing
defer = after parsing, in order; async = whenever ready, any order
Module scripts are deferred by default
Preload only the few resources that are critical and discovered late
pitfalls: Using async for scripts that depend on each other; their order isn't guaranteed.

quiz.q: app.js needs lib.js to have run first. Which loading keeps the order and doesn't block parsing?
options: Both as plain scripts at the top of head
quiz.explain: Deferred scripts run in document order after parsing; async scripts run in arrival order.

concepts.name: ARIA roles, states and live regions
concepts.summary: Use ARIA attributes to describe custom widgets and dynamic changes that native HTML can't express, and know when not to.
concepts.why: Custom components like tabs, menus and toasts are only accessible if their roles and states are exposed.
concepts.body:
**ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds attributes that change what assistive technology is told about an element. It changes semantics only, never behaviour: `role="button"` doesn't make a div focusable or keyboard-operable.

That's why the **first rule of ARIA** is: don't use it if a native element does the job. A `<button>` beats `<div role="button" tabindex="0">` plus key handlers every time.

When you do build custom widgets, ARIA comes in three kinds:

- **Roles**: what something is, e.g. `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"`, `role="tabpanel"`, `role="alert"`.
- **Properties**: relationships and names: `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`.
- **States**: current status, which your JavaScript must keep updating: `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-checked`, `aria-current="page"`, `aria-invalid`.

**Live regions** announce dynamic changes without moving focus. Put text into an element with `aria-live="polite"` (announced when the user is idle) or `role="alert"` (assertive, immediate) and screen readers read it. The region must exist in the DOM *before* you change its content.

`aria-hidden="true"` hides decorative content from assistive technology, but never put it on something focusable. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide documents the expected roles and keyboard patterns for tabs, menus, comboboxes and more; follow it rather than inventing your own.

takeaways: No ARIA is better than bad ARIA: prefer native elements
ARIA changes semantics only, not behaviour
Keep states like aria-expanded in sync from JavaScript
Live regions must exist before their content changes
pitfalls: Adding role="button" to a div and forgetting tabindex and Enter/Space handling.

quiz.q: What does adding role="button" to a <div> give you?
options: Focus, keyboard activation and the button role
Only the button role announced to assistive technology
quiz.explain: ARIA changes semantics only; focus and keyboard behaviour must be added by you.

concepts.name: Dialog, details and popover
concepts.summary: Build modals, disclosures and popups with native dialog, details/summary and the popover attribute instead of custom scripts.
concepts.why: Native interactive elements handle focus, Escape and stacking for you, which custom modals routinely get wrong.
concepts.body:
HTML now covers interactions that used to need a JavaScript library.

**details and summary** make a disclosure widget: `<summary>` is the always-visible toggle, the rest shows when `open`. No script required, keyboard accessible, searchable with find-in-page. Several `<details>` with the same `name` attribute form an exclusive accordion: opening one closes the others.

**dialog** is a native modal or non-modal box.

- `dialog.showModal()` opens it as a **modal**: it's placed in the **top layer** above everything, the rest of the page becomes inert, focus moves inside, and Escape closes it. Style the dimmed background with `::backdrop`.
- `dialog.show()` opens it non-modally; `dialog.close(value)` closes it.
- A `<form method="dialog">` inside closes the dialog on submit and sets `dialog.returnValue` to the submitting button's value.

**popover** is an attribute that turns any element into a popup in the top layer: `<div popover id="menu">`. A button with `popovertarget="menu"` toggles it, with no JavaScript. `popover` (auto) popovers light-dismiss: clicking outside or pressing Escape closes them, and opening one closes other auto popovers. `popover="manual"` stays open until closed explicitly, for toasts.

Prefer dialog for anything that demands a response, and popover for menus, tooltips and pickers. Both avoid z-index battles because the top layer always wins.

takeaways: details/summary = disclosure with no JS; shared name = accordion
showModal() gives top layer, inert background, Escape to close
form method="dialog" closes and sets returnValue
popover + popovertarget = light-dismiss popups with no JS
pitfalls: Opening a modal with dialog.show() and wondering why the page behind stays interactive.

quiz.q: What does a <form method="dialog"> inside a <dialog> do when submitted?
options: Closes the dialog and sets returnValue to the button's value
Sends a POST request to the current URL
quiz.explain: method=dialog closes the enclosing dialog without a network request.

concepts.name: Templates and custom elements
concepts.summary: Reuse markup with template and slot, and define your own tags with custom elements and shadow DOM.
concepts.why: Web components work in any framework or none, which makes them the native way to share UI widgets.
concepts.body:
**template** holds inert markup: it's parsed but not rendered, scripts inside don't run and images don't load. Clone its `.content` with `document.importNode` or `template.content.cloneNode(true)` to stamp out copies, which is faster and safer than building HTML strings.

**Custom elements** let you register new tags. A class extending `HTMLElement` is registered with `customElements.define("user-card", UserCard)`. Names must contain a hyphen, so they never clash with future HTML elements. Lifecycle callbacks run when the element is added (`connectedCallback`), removed (`disconnectedCallback`) or when an attribute listed in `static observedAttributes` changes (`attributeChangedCallback`).

**Shadow DOM** gives an element a private subtree: `this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" })`. Styles inside don't leak out and page styles don't leak in (inherited properties like `font` and custom properties still pass through). A `<slot>` in the shadow tree shows the element's light-DOM children; named slots (`<slot name="title">`) take children with a matching `slot` attribute.

You can also declare a shadow root in HTML with `<template shadowrootmode="open">`, so server-rendered components show up before any JavaScript runs.

Custom elements are upgraded when defined, so markup can appear before the script loads. Style the not-yet-defined state with the `:not(:defined)` selector to avoid a flash of unstyled content.
concepts.code: Ada Wrote the first program.
takeaways: template content is parsed but inert until cloned
Custom element names must contain a hyphen
Shadow DOM scopes styles; slots project the element's children
Declarative shadow DOM renders without JavaScript
pitfalls: Expecting global CSS classes to style elements inside a shadow root.

quiz.q: Why must custom element names contain a hyphen?
options: The parser uses it to detect void elements
So they can never collide with current or future standard elements
quiz.explain: Standard elements never contain hyphens, so hyphenated names are reserved for authors.

concepts.name: How browsers parse HTML
concepts.summary: Understand the HTML parser's error recovery, implied tags and tree construction, and how it differs from the DOM you write.
concepts.why: Knowing what the parser does explains phantom elements, broken templates and why innerHTML sometimes fails.
concepts.body:
HTML parsing is precisely specified, including how to handle broken markup, so every modern browser builds the same tree from the same bytes. That spec has a few behaviours every expert should know. **Tokenizer then tree builder.** Bytes are decoded (using the BOM, HTTP charset, or a `` found in the first 1024 bytes), tokenized into tags and text, and fed to a tree builder with **insertion modes** such as "in head", "in body" and "in table". **Implied tags.** The parser inserts ``, ``, `` and `` if missing, and many end tags are optional: `

`, ``, ``, `` close automatically when a sibling starts. **Error recovery.** Misnested formatting tags such as `` are repaired by the **adoption agency algorithm**. Content that can't go inside a table is **foster-parented**: it's moved before the table. That's why text typed between `` elements appears above the table. **Raw text elements.** Inside `` inside inline JavaScript ends the script early. Escape it as `<\/script>`. **Scripts pause parsing.** A classic script must run before parsing continues, because it might call `document.write`. The **preload scanner** looks ahead and starts fetching images and scripts anyway, which is why markup-declared resources load faster than ones injected by JavaScript. concepts.name: Loading performance in markup
concepts.summary: Tune how the browser prioritises and renders with fetchpriority, lazy loading, decoding hints and the critical rendering path.
concepts.why: Largest Contentful Paint and layout shift are mostly decided by how resources are declared in HTML.
concepts.body: The browser turns HTML into pixels through the **critical rendering path**: parse HTML into the DOM, fetch and parse CSS into the CSSOM (render-blocking), run blocking scripts, then lay out and paint. Your markup decides what lands on that path. **Priorities.** Browsers assign fetch priorities heuristically: CSS and blocking scripts high, images low until they're found to be in the viewport. `fetchpriority="high"` on the hero image tells the browser up front that it's the Largest Contentful Paint element; `fetchpriority="low"` demotes, say, off-screen carousel slides. It works on ``, ``, `
takeaways: Put the LCP image in the HTML with fetchpriority="high" and never lazy
The preload scanner can only find resources in markup
Sizes on media prevent layout shift
Measure LCP and CLS before and after changes
pitfalls: Setting the hero image as a CSS background, hiding it from the preload scanner.

quiz.q: Which change most likely improves LCP when the hero is ?
options: Moving the image into a CSS background
quiz.explain: Lazy loading delays the in-viewport hero; high priority fetches it first.

concepts.name: Form submission and constraint validation API
concepts.summary: Know exactly how forms encode and send data, and drive validation from JavaScript with the constraint validation API and FormData.
concepts.why: File uploads, custom error messages and progressive enhancement all depend on these details.
concepts.body:
When a form submits, the browser builds a list of entries from successful controls (named, enabled, checked if a checkbox or radio) and encodes them according to `enctype`:

- `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (default): `name=Ada+L&tags=a&tags=b`, spaces as `+`, other bytes percent-encoded. With `method="get"` this becomes the query string.
- `multipart/form-data`: each field in its own MIME part. Required for `<input type="file">`; with urlencoded only the file name is sent.
- `text/plain`: for debugging only; ambiguous to parse.

A submit button's `name=value` is included only for the button that was clicked, and buttons can override the form with `formaction`, `formmethod` and `formnovalidate`. Disabled controls are never sent; use `readonly` if the value must be submitted.

**The constraint validation API** exposes the browser's validation to scripts. Each control has `validity` (flags such as `valueMissing`, `patternMismatch`, `tooShort`, `customError`), `validationMessage`, `checkValidity()` and `reportValidity()`. `setCustomValidity("message")` marks a control invalid with your text; set it back to `""` or the field stays invalid forever. The `novalidate` attribute on the form disables native bubbles while keeping the API, which is how custom error UIs are built.

`new FormData(form)` captures exactly what a native submit would send, and `fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: formData })` sends it as multipart. Listening to the form's `submit` event and calling `requestSubmit()`, rather than `submit()`, keeps validation and submit handlers in play.
concepts.code:
<form id="f" action="/api/profile" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data" novalidate>
  <input name="username" required minlength="3">
  <input name="avatar" type="file" accept="image/*">
  <input name="confirm" placeholder="type DELETE">
  <button name="intent" value="save">Save</button>
</form>
<script>
  const f = document.getElementById("f");
  f.addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const c = f.elements.confirm;
    c.setCustomValidity(c.value === "DELETE" ? "" : "Type DELETE to confirm");
    if (!f.reportValidity()) return;      // shows first error, focuses it
    const data = new FormData(f, e.submitter); // includes intent=save
    const res = await fetch(f.action, { method: "POST", body: data });
    console.log(res.status);
  });
</script>
takeaways: File uploads need enctype="multipart/form-data"
Disabled controls are not submitted; readonly ones are
setCustomValidity("") clears a custom error
FormData(form, submitter) mirrors a native submit
pitfalls: Calling setCustomValidity with a message and never resetting it to an empty string.

quiz.q: A form with the default enctype has a file input. What does the server receive for it?
options: A multipart part with the file
quiz.explain: Only multipart/form-data carries file contents; urlencoded sends just the file name.
